title: Bhakti — the first use of the word in the Upanishads (6.23)
hook: the very last verse of the Shvetashvatara uses a word that will one day fill India's temples with song
carry: to one who has the highest devotion
tomorrow: Block A close · the seven Upanishads in one sit

segments.voice: Yesterday: the paradox. Smaller than small, greater than great, hidden in the heart and spread past the stars. Did you look from a tiny thing to the sky? Today, the Shvetashvatara's last word. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

Walk into a Hindu temple on a festival night and you may hear it before you see it: bells, drums, a crowd singing the same name over and over, someone in tears at the front. That whole world of love poured toward God has a name, bhakti, devotion. You met it in year one with Mirabai and the saints. But where does the word first show up in these old texts? You have to read to the very end of the Shvetashvatara, to its final verse, to find it.
screen: `BELLS, DRUMS, ONE NAME SUNG.` → `THE WORLD OF BHAKTI.` → `WHERE DOES THE WORD BEGIN?`

segments.voice: Verse 6.23, in paraphrase: for the great soul who has the highest devotion to God, and the same devotion to the teacher as to God, these things that have been taught shine out. They truly shine out for that great soul. The Sanskrit for highest devotion is para bhakti. The word bhakti comes from a root, bhaj, that means to share, to take part, to belong to. So devotion here isn't just a feeling. It's a share: you belong to God, and God is your portion. Scholars usually point to this verse as the first time the word bhakti appears in the principal Upanishads in this sense, devotion to a personal God. And it's a striking place to find it. This Upanishad has spent six chapters on the wheel, the swan, the fire sticks, the posture, Rudra the one Lord, the self smaller than small. And its final word on how all of that becomes real is not more knowledge. It's love. The teaching shines, the verse says, for the one who loves. Notice the teacher, too. Devotion to the guru as to God is part of the same verse, and many Hindu traditions honor the teacher this way. Not everyone reads it alike: Advaita teachers often treat devotion as what readies the mind for knowledge, while devotional schools treat it as the goal itself. Within a few centuries, the Bhagavad Gita will build a whole path out of this word.
screen: `PARA BHAKTI: THE HIGHEST DEVOTION.` · `BHAJ: TO SHARE, TO BELONG.` · `THE LAST VERSE IS ABOUT LOVE.` · then, large: `IT SHINES FOR THE ONE WHO LOVES.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone or something you love without needing anything back: a person, a teacher, a place, or, if you pray, God as you know God. Let that feeling sit in your chest. Don't push it bigger. Just notice what it does to the body, the shoulders, the breath, the face. Then notice that whatever you think about while that love is present looks a little different, a little brighter. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. Devotion, from a root that means to share or to belong. Its first appearance in the principal Upanishads is in the Shvetashvatara's last verse.
Your line: to one who has the highest devotion. Today, do one ordinary task out of love for someone, and notice whether it feels different from doing it out of duty. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Bhakti is lived across Hindu traditions through kirtan and bhajan singing, temple worship, repeating God's name, and honoring one's teacher, and many devotees treat love of God as the heart of practice.

fork.setup: six chapters of wheels, swans, fire sticks and paradoxes. what does the Shvetashvatara name, in its last verse, as what makes it all shine?
options: a better memory for the verses.
the highest devotion to God and the teacher.
fork.reveal: the teachings shine out for the great soul with para bhakti, the highest devotion. the last word is love.

original.note: Sanskrit bhakti: devotion, from bhaj, to share or belong. first used in this sense in the principal Upanishads at Shvetashvatara 6.23.

trapdoor: what you thought: bhakti means emotional worship.
what it means: belonging to God, sharing in God: a love that makes the teaching shine.
what a scholar hears: 6.23 is usually cited as the earliest Upanishadic use of bhakti for devotion to a personal God, a bridge to the Gita and the later bhakti movements.

sources.ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 6.23 (to one with the highest devotion to God and to the teacher, these things shine)

notes: 'First use of the word bhakti in the principal Upanishads' follows the outline and common scholarship; confirm, and whether it is the first use in this sense or at all.

Reference to Mirabai in year one assumes the year-one Hindu path covered her; confirm.
